chapter_text:
CHAPTER 8 — विरहकातरं तपोवनम् (VIRAHAKATARAM TAPOVANAM)

Introduction — पाठपरिचयः

This lesson, विरहकातरं तपोवनम् ("The Hermitage Distressed by Separation"), is retold from the fourth act (चतुर्थः अङ्कः) of Kalidasa's immortal play अभिज्ञानशाकुन्तलम् (Abhijnana-Shakuntalam, "The Recognition of Shakuntala"). Kalidasa (कालिदासः) is the greatest poet-dramatist of classical Sanskrit; his works are public domain and have been loved for over fifteen hundred years. The word विरह (viraha) means "separation" or the ache of parting; कातर (katara) means "distressed, timid, overcome"; तपोवनम् (tapovanam) is the "penance-grove" or hermitage. So the very title tells the theme: even the calm forest hermitage is overcome with grief when its beloved daughter leaves.

The setting — तपोवनस्य वर्णनम्

The story unfolds in the आश्रम (ashram, hermitage) of the sage कण्वः (Kanva) on the banks of the river मालिनी (Malini), near the foothills of the Himalayas. A तपोवन is a peaceful forest where sages (ऋषयः) perform penance (तपः), students (ब्रह्मचारिणः) study the Vedas, and where wild animals live without fear because no one harms them. In this loving atmosphere grew up शकुन्तला (Shakuntala), the foster-daughter of Kanva. She was raised among the trees (वृक्षाः), creepers (लताः), deer (मृगाः) and birds as if they were her own family. She watered the young saplings before drinking herself, she never plucked a tender leaf though she loved ornaments, and the first flowering of every plant was a festival (उत्सवः) for her. Nature and Shakuntala loved one another like kin.

The occasion — प्रसंगः

King दुष्यन्तः (Dushyanta) had met Shakuntala in the forest, married her by the गान्धर्व rite, and returned to his capital, giving her a ring (अङ्गुलीयकम्) as a token of recognition (अभिज्ञानम्). Now the time has come for Shakuntala, expecting her child, to leave the hermitage and go to her husband's home (पतिगृहम्). Act 4 is the "farewell act" — famous in all of Sanskrit literature as the विदाई (departure) of Shakuntala. It is here that the poet shows the तपोवन itself grieving.

The scene retold in simple Sanskrit — सरल-संस्कृते कथा

अद्य शकुन्तला पतिगृहं गमिष्यति। सर्वम् आश्रमम् एकः विषादः व्याप्नोति। कण्वः महर्षिः वृक्षान् सम्बोधयति — "हे वनस्पतयः! इयं शकुन्तला अद्य गच्छति। यूयम् एनां अनुजानीत।" (Today Shakuntala will go to her husband's house. A deep sadness pervades the whole hermitage. The great sage Kanva addresses the trees: "O trees! This Shakuntala goes today. Do all of you bid her farewell.")

वृक्षाः पुष्पाणि वर्षन्ति। कोकिलाः मधुरं कूजन्ति इव अनुज्ञां ददति। पवनः मन्दं वहति। (The trees rain down flowers; the cuckoos sing sweetly as if giving their leave; the wind blows gently.) मृग्यः तृणं न खादन्ति; मयूराः नृत्यं त्यजन्ति; लताः पाण्डुराणि पत्राणि मुञ्चन्ति — यथा ता अपि रोदन्ति। (The does no longer eat grass; the peacocks give up dancing; the creepers drop their pale leaves — as if they too are weeping.)

शकुन्तला अपि वनज्योत्स्नां लतां आलिङ्गति। सा मृगशिशुं यम् सा स्वयं पालितवती तम् आमन्त्रयते। तस्याः नेत्रे अश्रुपूर्णे भवतः। (Shakuntala embraces the jasmine-creeper Vanajyotsna. She takes leave of the fawn which she herself had reared. Her eyes fill with tears.) कण्वः स्नेहेन तां शिक्षां ददाति — "गुरून् शुश्रूषस्व, सपत्नीषु सखीवत् वर्तस्व, पतिम् अनुसर।" (Kanva lovingly instructs her: "Serve your elders, behave like a friend towards co-wives, follow your husband.")

एवं तपोवनं विरहेण कातरं भवति। न केवलं मनुष्याः, अपि तु वृक्षाः, लताः, मृगाः च शोकम् अनुभवन्ति। इयं कथा दर्शयति यत् मनुष्यस्य प्रकृत्या सह गाढः स्नेह-सम्बन्धः अस्ति। (Thus the hermitage is overcome by the grief of separation. Not only the humans, but the trees, creepers and deer too feel sorrow. This story shows that between a human being and Nature there is a deep bond of love.)

The verses — मूल-श्लोकाः (शब्दार्थ सहित)

1) पातुं न प्रथमं व्यवस्यति जलं युष्मास्वपीतेषु या
   नादत्ते प्रियमण्डनापि भवतां स्नेहेन या पल्लवम्।
   आद्ये वः कुसुमप्रसूतिसमये यस्या भवत्युत्सवः
   सेयं याति शकुन्तला पतिगृहं सर्वैरनुज्ञायताम्॥
   शब्दार्थ: पातुम् = to drink; न व्यवस्यति = does not resolve/venture; प्रथमम् = first; जलम् = water; युष्मासु अपीतेषु = while you (trees) are not yet watered; या = who; न आदत्ते = does not pluck; प्रियमण्डना अपि = though fond of ornament; भवताम् = your; स्नेहेन = out of affection; पल्लवम् = a tender leaf/shoot; आद्ये = at the first; वः = your; कुसुमप्रसूतिसमये = at the time of blossoming; यस्याः = of whom; भवति उत्सवः = there is a festival; सा इयम् = this very (Shakuntala); याति = goes; पतिगृहम् = to her husband's house; सर्वैः अनुज्ञायताम् = let her be given leave by all.
   Translation: "She who would not venture to drink water first while you were still unwatered; who, though fond of ornaments, never plucked a tender shoot of yours out of love; for whom the season of your first blossoming was a festival — that same Shakuntala now goes to her husband's home; may you all bid her farewell." (Kanva to the trees.)

2) यास्यत्यद्य शकुन्तलेति हृदयं संस्पृष्टमुत्कण्ठया
   कण्ठः स्तम्भितबाष्पवृत्तिकलुषश्चिन्ताजडं दर्शनम्।
   वैक्लव्यं मम तावदीदृशमिदं स्नेहादरण्यौकसः
   पीड्यन्ते गृहिणः कथं नु तनयाविश्लेषदुःखैर्नवैः॥
   शब्दार्थ: यास्यति अद्य = will go today; शकुन्तला इति = "Shakuntala (will go)"; हृदयम् = the heart; संस्पृष्टम् = is touched; उत्कण्ठया = by longing; कण्ठः = the throat; स्तम्भित-बाष्प-वृत्ति-कलुषः = choked by suppressed tears; चिन्ता-जडम् = dulled by anxiety; दर्शनम् = the sight/vision; वैक्लव्यम् = agitation, distress; मम = my; तावत् = even; ईदृशम् = such; स्नेहात् = out of affection; अरण्यौकसः = of a forest-dweller (ascetic); पीड्यन्ते = are afflicted; गृहिणः = householders; कथं नु = how indeed; तनया-विश्लेष-दुःखैः = by the sorrows of parting from a daughter; नवैः = fresh/new.
   Translation: "'Today Shakuntala will go' — at this thought my heart is gripped by longing, my throat is choked with held-back tears, my sight is dulled by care. If even I, a forest ascetic, am so shaken by love, how much more must householders be tormented by the fresh grief of parting from a daughter!" (Kanva.)

3) उद्गलितदर्भकवला मृग्यः परित्यक्तनर्तना मयूराः।
   अपसृतपाण्डुपत्रा मुञ्चन्त्यश्रूणीव लताः॥
   शब्दार्थ: उद्गलित-दर्भ-कवलाः = (does) whose mouthful of darbha grass has slipped out; मृग्यः = the does; परित्यक्त-नर्तनाः = who have given up dancing; मयूराः = the peacocks; अपसृत-पाण्डु-पत्राः = who have shed their pale leaves; मुञ्चन्ति = release, let fall; अश्रूणि इव = as if tears; लताः = the creepers.
   Translation: "The does let the mouthfuls of darbha grass slip from their mouths, the peacocks have given up their dancing, and the creepers, shedding their pale leaves, seem to be letting fall tears." Even the animals and plants share the grief of parting.

4) शुश्रूषस्व गुरून् कुरु प्रियसखीवृत्तिं सपत्नीजने
   पत्युर्विप्रकृतापि रोषणतया मा स्म प्रतीपं गमः।
   भूयिष्ठं भव दक्षिणा परिजने भाग्येष्वनुत्सेकिनी
   यान्त्येवं गृहिणीपदं युवतयो वामाः कुलस्याधयः॥
   शब्दार्थ: शुश्रूषस्व = serve, obey; गुरून् = elders; कुरु = do, adopt; प्रियसखी-वृत्तिम् = the conduct of a dear friend; सपत्नीजने = towards co-wives; पत्युः = by the husband; विप्रकृता अपि = even if wronged/offended; रोषणतया = through angry temper; मा स्म प्रतीपं गमः = do not go against (him); भूयिष्ठम् = mostly, ever; भव = be; दक्षिणा = courteous, kind; परिजने = towards attendants; भाग्येषु = in (times of) fortune; अनुत्सेकिनी = not arrogant; यान्ति एवम् = thus attain; गृहिणी-पदम् = the rank of a housewife; युवतयः = young women; वामाः = the perverse/wayward ones; कुलस्य आधयः = are afflictions of the family.
   Translation: "Serve your elders; treat your co-wives as dear friends; even if wronged by your husband, do not turn against him out of anger; be ever courteous to attendants and never proud in good fortune. Young women who behave so attain the honoured rank of the mistress of a house; the wayward ones are but a burden on their family." (Kanva's parting counsel to Shakuntala.)

The moral — सन्देशः

The chapter's central message is the deep, mutual love (स्नेहः) between human beings and Nature (प्रकृतिः). Shakuntala cared for the plants and animals as her own kin, and so, at her departure, they grieve as a family grieves. The lesson for us is to see Nature not as a lifeless thing to be used, but as a living companion deserving love and protection — a truly modern message of environmental sensitivity taught by an ancient poet. The chapter also teaches, through Kanva's counsel, the virtues of duty, humility, patience and courtesy that make a good life.

व्याकरणम् — Grammar from the lesson (English explanation, Devanagari examples)

(A) सन्धि (Sandhi — the joining of sounds).
  • यास्यति + अद्य → यास्यत्यद्य (इ + अ = य्, यण्-सन्धि). Split back: यास्यति + अद्य.
  • न + आदत्ते → नादत्ते (अ + आ = आ, दीर्घ-सन्धि).
  • मुञ्चन्ति + अश्रूणि → मुञ्चन्त्यश्रूणि (इ + अ = य्, यण्-सन्धि).
  • सा + इयम् → सेयम् (आ + इ = ए, गुण-सन्धि).
  • स्नेहात् + अरण्यौकसः → स्नेहादरण्यौकसः (त् → द् before a vowel, व्यञ्जन-सन्धि).
Splitting a joined form back into its parts (सन्धि-विच्छेदः) is a key reading skill.

(B) विभक्ति (Vibhakti — case endings). Using the masculine a-stem वृक्ष (tree) as a model:
  • प्रथमा (nominative, subject): वृक्षः — the doer; in the verses शकुन्तला, मृग्यः, मयूराः, लताः are subjects.
  • द्वितीया (accusative, object): वृक्षम् — what is acted on; जलम् "water", पल्लवम् "a shoot", वृक्षान् "the trees" (object of सम्बोधयति).
  • तृतीया (instrumental, "by/with"): वृक्षेण; उत्कण्ठया "by longing", स्नेहेन "out of affection", सर्वैः "by all".
  • पञ्चमी (ablative, "from"): वृक्षात्; स्नेहात् "out of/from affection".
  • षष्ठी (genitive, "of"): वृक्षस्य; यस्याः "of whom", कुलस्य "of the family", भवताम् "your (of you)".
  • सप्तमी (locative, "in/at/on"): वृक्षे; युष्मासु "among you", सपत्नीजने "towards/among co-wives", समये "at the time".

(C) शब्दरूप (declension — worked examples). The a-stem masculine वृक्ष (प्रथमा): एकवचन वृक्षः, द्विवचन वृक्षौ, बहुवचन वृक्षाः. The आ-stem feminine लता (प्रथमा): एकवचन लता, द्विवचन लते, बहुवचन लताः. Notice मृग्यः (does) and मयूराः (peacocks) are plural nominatives — "many" of each.

(D) धातुरूप (conjugation — worked example). The root गम् (to go, गच्छ्) in लट्-लकार (present tense), परस्मैपद:
  एकवचन — गच्छति (he/she goes), गच्छसि (you go), गच्छामि (I go);
  द्विवचन — गच्छतः, गच्छथः, गच्छावः;
  बहुवचन — गच्छन्ति (they go), गच्छथ, गच्छामः.
From this root come याति / यास्यति "goes / will go" (a synonym, root या) used of Shakuntala, and गमिष्यति "will go" (लृट्-लकार, future).

SUMMARY (सारांश)

In this chapter you read विरहकातरं तपोवनम्, retold from Act 4 of Kalidasa's अभिज्ञानशाकुन्तलम्. You learned about the तपोवन — the peaceful hermitage of sage Kanva where Shakuntala grew up loving the trees, creepers and deer as her own family. When the day comes for her to leave for her husband Dushyanta's home, the whole hermitage is overcome with grief (विरह): the trees shower flowers, the does drop their grass, the peacocks stop dancing, and the creepers shed pale leaves like tears. You studied four authentic public-domain verses — Kanva's appeal to the trees (पातुं न प्रथमम्...), his own anguish (यास्यत्यद्य शकुन्तला...), the grieving of the animals and plants (उद्गलितदर्भकवलाः...), and his tender parting counsel (शुश्रूषस्व गुरून्...) — each with शब्दार्थ and English translation. The great theme is the loving bond between human beings and Nature, and the duty to cherish and protect the natural world. Finally you drew grammar from the lesson: यण्, दीर्घ, गुण and व्यञ्जन सन्धि (with सन्धि-विच्छेद), the six विभक्ति case endings, the शब्दरूप of वृक्ष and लता, and the धातुरूप of गम् in the present tense.

topics.name: तपोवनम् — The Hermitage and its Setting
topics.description: The peaceful penance-grove (तपोवन) of sage Kanva on the Malini river where Shakuntala grew up; life among sages, students and fearless animals, and the play अभिज्ञानशाकुन्तलम् from which the lesson is retold.

topics.name: विरह-प्रसंगः — The Scene of Separation
topics.description: The occasion of Shakuntala's departure to her husband Dushyanta's home (पतिगृहम्); Act 4 as the famous farewell (विदाई) of Shakuntala and the sorrow that spreads through the whole ashram.

topics.name: प्रकृतेः शोकः — Nature and the Ashram Grieving
topics.description: How the trees, creepers, does and peacocks share the grief of parting — trees showering flowers, does dropping darbha grass, peacocks ceasing to dance, creepers shedding pale leaves like tears.

topics.name: शब्दार्थ — Word Meanings and Vocabulary
topics.description: Building Sanskrit vocabulary from the verses: विरह, कातर, तपोवन, पल्लव, अश्रु, स्नेह, उत्कण्ठा, लता, मृगी, मयूर, पतिगृह and their English meanings and case-forms.

topics.name: सन्देशः — Message, Morals and Kanva's Counsel
topics.description: The central theme of loving bond between human beings and Nature and the duty to protect it; and Kanva's parting counsel of duty, humility, patience and courtesy (शुश्रूषस्व गुरून्...).

topics.name: व्याकरणम् — Grammar (Sandhi, Vibhakti, Shabda-rupa, Dhatu-rupa)
topics.description: Grammar drawn from the lesson: यण्/दीर्घ/गुण/व्यञ्जन सन्धि with सन्धि-विच्छेद, the six विभक्ति case endings, the शब्दरूप of वृक्ष and लता, and the धातुरूप of गम् (गच्छति) in लट्-लकार.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: तपोवनम् — The Hermitage and its Setting
learning_outcomes.description: Explain what a तपोवन is and describe the setting of Kanva's hermitage and the play अभिज्ञानशाकुन्तलम् from which the lesson is taken.
Recall the occasion of Shakuntala's departure to her husband's home and identify the main characters (शकुन्तला, कण्वः, दुष्यन्तः) and events of the farewell scene.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: प्रकृतेः शोकः — Nature and the Ashram Grieving
learning_outcomes.description: Explain how the trees, creepers, does and peacocks of the hermitage share in the grief of Shakuntala's departure.
Give the शब्दार्थ (word meaning) in English of Sanskrit words drawn from the lesson and use the vocabulary correctly.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: सन्देशः — Message, Morals and Kanva's Counsel
learning_outcomes.description: Analyse the theme of the loving bond between human beings and Nature and Kanva's counsel, and apply the lessons to modern life and environmental care.
Identify and perform simple सन्धि joins and splits (सन्धि-विच्छेद) using examples taken from the verses of the lesson.
Recognise the six विभक्ति case endings, the शब्दरूप of वृक्ष and लता, and the धातुरूप of गम्, and state the case or form of a word from the lesson.
Translate a given verse of the lesson into simple English and answer comprehension questions about its words, grammar and meaning.

chapter_summary.title: विरहकातरं तपोवनम् (Virahakataram Tapovanam) — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Secondary Sanskrit (209) summary for Chapter 8, retold from Act 4 of Kalidasa's अभिज्ञानशाकुन्तलम्. It describes the तपोवन (hermitage) grieving as Shakuntala departs for her husband's home, presents four public-domain verses with their meanings, and draws simple grammar from the text.

In शुश्रूषस्व गुरून्..., Kanva counsels duty to elders, friendship to co-wives, patience with the husband, courtesy and humility.

sections.heading: Grammar from the lesson
bullets: यण्-सन्धि: यास्यति + अद्य = यास्यत्यद्य (इ + अ = य्); मुञ्चन्ति + अश्रूणि = मुञ्चन्त्यश्रूणि.
दीर्घ/गुण/व्यञ्जन सन्धि: न + आदत्ते = नादत्ते; सा + इयम् = सेयम्; स्नेहात् + अरण्यौकसः = स्नेहादरण्यौकसः.
विभक्ति: तृतीया स्नेहेन 'by affection', पञ्चमी स्नेहात् 'from affection', सप्तमी युष्मासु 'among you'.
शब्दरूप वृक्ष: वृक्षः/वृक्षौ/वृक्षाः; लता: लता/लते/लताः. धातुरूप गम्: गच्छति, गच्छतः, गच्छन्ति.

key_takeaways: विरहकातरं तपोवनम् is retold from Act 4 of Kalidasa's अभिज्ञानशाकुन्तलम् — the famous farewell of Shakuntala.
A तपोवन is a peaceful hermitage where Shakuntala grew up loving the trees, creepers and deer as her family.
When Shakuntala leaves for her husband's home, the whole hermitage is overcome with the grief of separation (विरह).
Nature shares the sorrow: trees shower flowers, does drop their grass, peacocks stop dancing, creepers shed leaves like tears.
The central message is the deep loving bond between humans and Nature, and the duty to protect the natural world.
Kanva's counsel (शुश्रूषस्व गुरून्...) teaches duty, humility, patience and courtesy.
Grammar: यण्-सन्धि (यास्यति+अद्य=यास्यत्यद्य), the six विभक्ति endings, and the धातुरूप of गम् (गच्छति).

glossary.definition: Separation; the ache or grief of parting from a loved one — the theme of the chapter.
Distressed, timid, overcome (by emotion); here the hermitage is कातर with grief.
A penance-grove or hermitage where sages perform तपः and animals live without fear.
The hermitage; the dwelling of a sage and his students, here that of sage Kanva.
Kalidasa's celebrated Sanskrit play, 'The Recognition of Shakuntala', from Act 4 of which this lesson is retold.
The foster-daughter of sage Kanva, wife of King Dushyanta, who departs for her husband's home.
The sage and foster-father of Shakuntala who bids her a grief-stricken farewell.
The husband's house/home, to which Shakuntala departs from the hermitage.
Affection, love; the bond between Shakuntala and the plants and animals of the hermitage.
A tender leaf or young shoot; Shakuntala never plucked one out of love for the trees.
A tear; the creepers shed pale leaves 'like tears' (अश्रूणि इव).
A creeper or vine; Shakuntala embraced the jasmine-creeper Vanajyotsna before leaving.
A doe; the does drop their mouthfuls of darbha grass in grief (मृग्यः, plural).
Leave, permission, farewell; Kanva asks the trees to grant Shakuntala their अनुज्ञा.
Longing, yearning; Kanva's heart is touched by उत्कण्ठा at Shakuntala's departure.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
पातुं न प्रथमं व्यवस्यति जलं युष्मास्वपीतेषु या
नादत्ते प्रियमण्डनापि भवतां स्नेहेन या पल्लवम्।
(a) What would Shakuntala not do first? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'पल्लवम्'. (c) What does this show about her?
questions.answer: (a) She would not drink water first while the trees were still unwatered. (b) पल्लवम् = a tender leaf/shoot. (c) It shows her deep love and care for the trees, as for her own family.

questions.question: Discuss the theme of love between human beings and Nature in this chapter and its message for today.
questions.answer: Shakuntala loved the forest as family — watering saplings before drinking, never plucking a shoot, celebrating each flowering. In return the trees shower flowers, the does drop their grass, the peacocks stop dancing and the creepers shed leaves like tears at her departure. Kalidasa personifies Nature to show that love given to it is returned. The message for us is to treat Nature as a living companion and to cherish and protect it — an ancient vision of ecological harmony that is urgently relevant today.

questions.question: Explain Kanva's parting counsel to Shakuntala (शुश्रूषस्व गुरून्...) and the values it teaches.
questions.answer: Kanva advises Shakuntala to serve her elders, treat her co-wives as dear friends, not turn against her husband in anger even if wronged, be courteous to attendants, and never be proud in good fortune. Such a woman attains the honoured rank of a householder; the wayward become a burden on the family. The counsel teaches duty, patience, humility, friendliness and courtesy.

What is a तपोवन? Give one feature of it.
questions.answer: A तपोवन is a peaceful forest hermitage where sages (ऋषयः) perform penance (तपः) and students study. One feature: the wild animals live there without fear because no one harms them.
questions.explanation: Definition of तपोवन plus a feature.

questions.question: From which work and which act is 'विरहकातरं तपोवनम्' taken?
questions.answer: It is retold from the fourth act (चतुर्थः अङ्कः) of Kalidasa's play अभिज्ञानशाकुन्तलम्.

questions.question: Explain the meaning of the title 'विरहकातरं तपोवनम्'.
questions.answer: विरह = separation, कातर = distressed/overcome, तपोवनम् = the hermitage. Together the title means 'the hermitage overcome by the grief of separation' — the ashram distressed as Shakuntala leaves.

questions.question: Why is Shakuntala leaving the hermitage?
questions.answer: She is leaving because she is now married to King Dushyanta and the time has come for her to go to her husband's home (पतिगृहम्).

questions.question: Describe the mood of the ashram on the day Shakuntala departs.
questions.answer: A deep sadness (विषादः) pervades the whole ashram. Kanva is grief-stricken, Shakuntala's eyes fill with tears, and even the trees, does, peacocks and creepers seem to mourn. The joyful hermitage becomes कातर (distressed) with the grief of parting.

questions.question: Whom does Kanva address in the first verse, and what does he ask?
questions.answer: Kanva addresses the trees (वनस्पतयः) of the hermitage. He tells them that Shakuntala, who loved and cared for them, is now leaving for her husband's home, and he asks them all to give her their leave (अनुज्ञा).

questions.question: How do the animals and plants of the hermitage show their grief?
questions.answer: The does (मृग्यः) let the mouthfuls of darbha grass slip from their mouths; the peacocks (मयूराः) give up their dancing; and the creepers (लताः) shed their pale leaves as if shedding tears. Even the trees shower flowers as a farewell.
questions.explanation: Nature's grief in the verse उद्गलित-दर्भ-कवलाः...

questions.question: Why does Nature grieve so deeply at Shakuntala's departure?
questions.answer: Because Shakuntala had loved and cared for the plants and animals as her own family — watering the saplings before drinking herself, never plucking a tender shoot, and celebrating each first flowering. Nature returns her love, and so grieves at her going as a family grieves.

questions.question: Give two ways in which Shakuntala had cared for the trees.
questions.answer: (1) She would not drink water first while the young trees were still unwatered. (2) Though fond of ornaments, she never plucked even a tender shoot (पल्लव) out of love for them.
questions.explanation: Two acts of care from verse 1.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ of: विरहः, स्नेहः, पल्लवः, अश्रु.
questions.answer: विरहः = separation; स्नेहः = affection/love; पल्लवः = a tender leaf/shoot; अश्रु = a tear.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ of: लता, मृगी, मयूरः, पतिगृहम्.
questions.answer: लता = creeper/vine; मृगी = doe; मयूरः = peacock; पतिगृहम् = the husband's home.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ of: उत्कण्ठा, अनुज्ञा, उत्सवः.
questions.answer: उत्कण्ठा = longing/yearning; अनुज्ञा = leave/permission/farewell; उत्सवः = festival.

questions.question: What is the central message of the chapter?
questions.answer: The central message is the deep, mutual bond of love (स्नेहः) between human beings and Nature. Because Shakuntala loved the trees, creepers and animals as kin, they grieve at her departure. The chapter teaches us to see Nature as a living companion and to cherish and protect it.

questions.question: How is this ancient chapter relevant to today's environmental concerns?
questions.answer: The chapter shows a human being who treated plants and animals with love and never harmed them, and a Nature that loved her back. This is exactly the attitude modern environmental care needs — to respect, protect and live in harmony with the natural world rather than exploiting it. Kalidasa thus gives an ancient but strikingly modern message of ecological sensitivity.
questions.explanation: Links the theme to modern ecology.

questions.question: Summarise Kanva's parting counsel to Shakuntala.
questions.answer: Kanva advises Shakuntala to serve her elders (शुश्रूषस्व गुरून्), to treat her co-wives as dear friends, not to turn against her husband in anger even if wronged, to be courteous to attendants, and never to be proud in good fortune. Such conduct, he says, wins a woman the honoured place of a householder.

questions.question: Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद (split) of: (a) यास्यत्यद्य (b) नादत्ते.
questions.answer: (a) यास्यत्यद्य = यास्यति + अद्य (इ + अ = य्, यण्-सन्धि). (b) नादत्ते = न + आदत्ते (अ + आ = आ, दीर्घ-सन्धि).

questions.question: Join by सन्धि: (a) सा + इयम् (b) मुञ्चन्ति + अश्रूणि.
questions.answer: (a) सा + इयम् = सेयम् (आ + इ = ए, गुण-सन्धि). (b) मुञ्चन्ति + अश्रूणि = मुञ्चन्त्यश्रूणि (इ + अ = य्, यण्-सन्धि).

questions.question: State the विभक्ति (case) and role of: स्नेहेन, स्नेहात्, युष्मासु.
questions.answer: स्नेहेन = तृतीया (instrumental) → 'by/out of affection'. स्नेहात् = पञ्चमी (ablative) → 'from/out of affection'. युष्मासु = सप्तमी (locative) → 'among/in you'.

questions.question: Give the शब्दरूप (प्रथमा, all three numbers) of लता.
questions.answer: लता (feminine, आ-stem), प्रथमा: एकवचन लता, द्विवचन लते, बहुवचन लताः.

questions.question: Give the धातुरूप of गम् (लट्-लकार) in the third person, all three numbers.
questions.answer: गम् (root, गच्छ्), लट्-लकार, प्रथम-पुरुष: एकवचन गच्छति, द्विवचन गच्छतः, बहुवचन गच्छन्ति.

questions.question: Translate into English: 'सेयं याति शकुन्तला पतिगृहं सर्वैरनुज्ञायताम्'.
questions.answer: 'That same Shakuntala now goes to her husband's home; may she be given leave (farewell) by you all.' Kanva asks the trees to bid Shakuntala a loving farewell.
questions.explanation: Translation of the close of verse 1.

questions.question: In the verse 'यास्यत्यद्य शकुन्तला...', how does Kanva contrast his own grief with that of householders?
questions.answer: Kanva says that even he, a detached forest ascetic (अरण्यौकस्), is so shaken by grief — his heart gripped by longing, throat choked with tears, sight dulled by care — that householders (गृहिणः), who are far more attached, must suffer immeasurably more from the fresh pain of parting from a daughter (तनया-विश्लेष-दुःख).
questions.explanation: Contrast of ascetic vs householder grief.

questions.question: Describe the तपोवन of sage Kanva and the place of Shakuntala in it.
questions.answer: The तपोवन is the peaceful forest hermitage of sage Kanva, set on the bank of the river Malini near the Himalayan foothills. In it sages perform penance (तपः), young students study the Vedas, and wild animals move about without fear, since no one harms them. In this loving, gentle atmosphere grew up Shakuntala, the foster-daughter of Kanva. She was raised among the trees, creepers, deer and birds as though they were her own family: she watered the saplings before drinking herself, never plucked a tender shoot though she loved ornaments, and treated the first flowering of every plant as a festival. Thus the hermitage and Shakuntala were bound by mutual love, which is why her departure grieves the whole तपोवन.
questions.explanation: Setting of the hermitage and Shakuntala's bond with it.

questions.question: Narrate the scene of Shakuntala's farewell from the hermitage.
questions.answer: On the appointed day Shakuntala must leave the hermitage for the home of her husband, King Dushyanta. A deep sadness spreads through the whole ashram. Sage Kanva addresses the trees, telling them that the girl who loved and cared for them is now leaving, and asks them to give her their farewell. The trees shower down flowers and the cuckoos sing sweetly as if bidding her leave. The does stop eating grass, the peacocks give up dancing, and the creepers shed pale leaves like tears. Shakuntala embraces the jasmine-creeper Vanajyotsna and takes leave of the fawn she had reared, her eyes filling with tears. Then Kanva lovingly gives her his parting counsel and sends her off. Thus the whole तपोवन becomes कातर — overcome — with the grief of separation.
questions.explanation: Full narration of the departure scene.

questions.question: Using the verse 'उद्गलितदर्भकवला मृग्यः...', explain how Nature shares Shakuntala's grief and what this reveals.
questions.answer: The verse says: the does (मृग्यः) let the mouthfuls of darbha grass slip from their mouths, the peacocks (मयूराः) have given up their dancing, and the creepers (लताः), shedding their pale leaves, seem to be letting fall tears. Every image shows a creature or plant halting its natural, happy activity out of sorrow — the doe forgets to eat, the peacock forgets to dance, the creeper 'weeps'. This reveals that the bond between Shakuntala and Nature was mutual and deep: she had loved and protected them as family, and now they mourn her as family would. The poet thus personifies Nature to show that love given to the natural world is returned, and that human beings and Nature belong to one living, feeling community. It is a profound lesson in compassion and environmental love.
questions.explanation: Analysis of Nature's grief and its meaning.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ of at least eight important words from the lesson.
questions.answer: विरहः = separation; कातरः = distressed/overcome; तपोवनम् = hermitage; स्नेहः = affection; पल्लवः = tender shoot; अश्रु = tear; लता = creeper; मृगी = doe; मयूरः = peacock; उत्कण्ठा = longing; अनुज्ञा = leave/farewell; पतिगृहम् = husband's home.

questions.question: Discuss the theme of love between human beings and Nature in this chapter and its message for us today.
questions.answer: The chapter's great theme is the mutual bond of love (स्नेहः) between human beings and Nature. Shakuntala did not merely live in the forest; she loved it. She watered the young trees before drinking herself, never plucked a tender leaf though she loved ornaments, and celebrated each plant's first flowering. In return, at her departure, the trees shower flowers, the does drop their grass, the peacocks cease dancing and the creepers shed leaves like tears. Kalidasa personifies Nature to show that it feels and responds to human love. For us today this carries a powerful message: the natural world is not a lifeless resource to be exploited, but a living companion to be respected, cherished and protected. In an age of pollution and deforestation, the chapter's ancient vision of harmony between humans and Nature is strikingly modern and urgently needed. To love and guard Nature is, the poet suggests, part of being truly human.
questions.explanation: Evaluation of the human-Nature theme and its modern relevance.

questions.question: Explain Kanva's parting counsel to Shakuntala and the values it teaches.
questions.answer: In the verse 'शुश्रूषस्व गुरून्...', Kanva counsels Shakuntala on how to live in her husband's home. She should serve and obey her elders (शुश्रूषस्व गुरून्); treat her co-wives as dear friends rather than rivals (प्रियसखीवृत्तिं सपत्नीजने); not turn against her husband in anger even if she is wronged (रोषणतया मा स्म प्रतीपं गमः); be ever courteous to the attendants (दक्षिणा परिजने); and never grow proud in good fortune (भाग्येषु अनुत्सेकिनी). Such a woman, he says, attains the honoured rank of the mistress of a house, while the wayward become a burden on the family. The counsel teaches enduring values of duty, patience, humility, friendliness and courtesy.

questions.question: Explain सन्धि and सन्धि-विच्छेद with four examples taken from the verses of this chapter.
questions.answer: सन्धि is the joining/merging of sounds where two words meet; सन्धि-विच्छेद is splitting such a joined form back into its parts. Examples from the lesson: (1) यास्यति + अद्य = यास्यत्यद्य (इ + अ = य्, यण्-सन्धि); (2) मुञ्चन्ति + अश्रूणि = मुञ्चन्त्यश्रूणि (इ + अ = य्, यण्-सन्धि); (3) न + आदत्ते = नादत्ते (अ + आ = आ, दीर्घ-सन्धि); (4) सा + इयम् = सेयम् (आ + इ = ए, गुण-सन्धि). Being able both to join (सन्धि) and to split (सन्धि-विच्छेद) is essential for reading Sanskrit verses correctly.
questions.explanation: Definition plus four worked sandhi examples.

questions.question: Explain the six विभक्ति (cases) with one example each drawn from the lesson.
questions.answer: Sanskrit nouns change their ending to show their role: 1. प्रथमा (nominative, subject): शकुन्तला 'Shakuntala', मयूराः 'peacocks'. 2. द्वितीया (accusative, object): जलम् 'water', वृक्षान् 'the trees'. 3. तृतीया (instrumental, 'by'): स्नेहेन 'out of affection', सर्वैः 'by all'. 4. पञ्चमी (ablative, 'from'): स्नेहात् 'from affection'. 5. षष्ठी (genitive, 'of'): यस्याः 'of whom', कुलस्य 'of the family'. 6. सप्तमी (locative, 'in/among'): युष्मासु 'among you', समये 'at the time'. Recognising these endings tells us who does what in a verse.

questions.question:
Read the verse and answer:
पातुं न प्रथमं व्यवस्यति जलं युष्मास्वपीतेषु या
नादत्ते प्रियमण्डनापि भवतां स्नेहेन या पल्लवम्।
(a) What would Shakuntala not do before the trees were watered? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'पल्लवम्'. (c) In which विभक्ति is 'स्नेहेन'? (d) What does this tell us about Shakuntala?
questions.answer: (a) She would not venture to drink water first while the trees were still unwatered. (b) पल्लवम् = a tender leaf/shoot. (c) स्नेहेन is तृतीया (instrumental) — 'out of affection'. (d) It tells us Shakuntala loved and cared for the trees as her own family.
questions.explanation: Comprehension of Shakuntala's care for the trees.

questions.question:
Read the verse and answer:
आद्ये वः कुसुमप्रसूतिसमये यस्या भवत्युत्सवः
सेयं याति शकुन्तला पतिगृहं सर्वैरनुज्ञायताम्।
(a) What was a festival for Shakuntala? (b) Where is Shakuntala going? (c) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'अनुज्ञायताम्'. (d) Whom is Kanva addressing?
questions.answer: (a) The first blossoming (कुसुम-प्रसूति) of the plants was a festival (उत्सवः) for her. (b) She is going to her husband's home (पतिगृहम्). (c) अनुज्ञायताम् = 'let (her) be given leave/farewell'. (d) Kanva is addressing the trees of the hermitage.
questions.explanation: Comprehension of the farewell appeal to the trees.

questions.question:
Read the verse and answer:
उद्गलितदर्भकवला मृग्यः परित्यक्तनर्तना मयूराः।
अपसृतपाण्डुपत्रा मुञ्चन्त्यश्रूणीव लताः॥
(a) What do the does let slip from their mouths? (b) What have the peacocks given up? (c) Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद of 'मुञ्चन्त्यश्रूणि'. (d) What is the effect the poet creates?
questions.answer: (a) The does let their mouthful of darbha grass slip out. (b) The peacocks have given up their dancing. (c) मुञ्चन्त्यश्रूणि = मुञ्चन्ति + अश्रूणि. (d) By showing animals and plants halting their happy activities in sorrow, the poet makes all of Nature seem to weep with grief at Shakuntala's departure.
questions.explanation: Comprehension with a sandhi split; Nature's grief.

questions.question:
Read the verse and answer:
यास्यत्यद्य शकुन्तलेति हृदयं संस्पृष्टमुत्कण्ठया
कण्ठः स्तम्भितबाष्पवृत्तिकलुषश्चिन्ताजडं दर्शनम्।
(a) What thought grips Kanva's heart? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'उत्कण्ठा'. (c) Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद of 'यास्यत्यद्य'. (d) How is Kanva's throat described?
questions.answer: (a) The thought 'Today Shakuntala will go' (यास्यति अद्य शकुन्तला). (b) उत्कण्ठा = longing/yearning. (c) यास्यत्यद्य = यास्यति + अद्य. (d) His throat is choked with held-back tears (स्तम्भित-बाष्प-वृत्ति-कलुषः).

questions.question:
Read the verse and answer:
वैक्लव्यं मम तावदीदृशमिदं स्नेहादरण्यौकसः
पीड्यन्ते गृहिणः कथं नु तनयाविश्लेषदुःखैर्नवैः॥
(a) Who is speaking, and how does he describe himself? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'गृहिणः'. (c) In which विभक्ति is 'स्नेहात्'? (d) What point is Kanva making?
questions.answer: (a) Sage Kanva is speaking; he describes himself as an अरण्यौकस् — a forest-dweller/ascetic. (b) गृहिणः = householders. (c) स्नेहात् is पञ्चमी (ablative) — 'out of affection'. (d) Kanva reasons that if even he, a detached forest ascetic, is so shaken by grief, how much more must householders suffer the fresh pain of parting from a daughter.
questions.explanation: Comprehension of Kanva's reflection on parting.

questions.question:
Read the verse and answer:
शुश्रूषस्व गुरून् कुरु प्रियसखीवृत्तिं सपत्नीजने
पत्युर्विप्रकृतापि रोषणतया मा स्म प्रतीपं गमः।
(a) How should Shakuntala treat her elders? (b) How should she treat her co-wives? (c) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'शुश्रूषस्व'. (d) What should she not do even if wronged?
questions.answer: (a) She should serve and obey her elders. (b) She should treat her co-wives as dear friends (प्रियसखी). (c) शुश्रूषस्व = 'serve/obey'. (d) Even if wronged by her husband, she should not turn against him out of anger.

questions.question:
Read the verse and answer:
भूयिष्ठं भव दक्षिणा परिजने भाग्येष्वनुत्सेकिनी
यान्त्येवं गृहिणीपदं युवतयो वामाः कुलस्याधयः॥
(a) How should Shakuntala behave towards attendants? (b) What should she avoid in good fortune? (c) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'गृहिणीपदम्'. (d) What does Kanva say about wayward women?
questions.answer: (a) She should be ever courteous and kind (दक्षिणा) towards attendants. (b) She should avoid being proud/arrogant (अनुत्सेकिनी) in good fortune. (c) गृहिणीपदम् = the rank/position of the mistress of a house. (d) Wayward (वाम) women, he says, become a burden or affliction (आधि) on their family.
questions.explanation: Comprehension of the values in Kanva's counsel.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
वृक्षाः पुष्पाणि वर्षन्ति। लताः पाण्डुराणि पत्राणि मुञ्चन्ति। मृग्यः तृणं न खादन्ति।
(a) What do the trees do? (b) Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद of 'नादत्ते' from the verses. (c) In which विभक्ति is 'पुष्पाणि'? (d) What overall picture is drawn?
questions.answer: (a) The trees shower down flowers (पुष्पाणि वर्षन्ति). (b) नादत्ते = न + आदत्ते. (c) पुष्पाणि is द्वितीया (accusative, object of वर्षन्ति) — 'flowers'. (d) The whole hermitage — trees, creepers and does alike — is pictured mourning Shakuntala's departure.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
अद्य शकुन्तला पतिगृहं गच्छति। कण्वः वृक्षान् सम्बोधयति।
(a) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'पतिगृहम्'. (b) Identify the धातुरूप 'गच्छति' — its root, tense and person. (c) In which विभक्ति is 'वृक्षान्'? (d) Who addresses the trees?
questions.answer: (a) पतिगृहम् = the husband's home. (b) गच्छति is from root गम्, लट्-लकार (present tense), प्रथम-पुरुष एकवचन (third person singular). (c) वृक्षान् is द्वितीया (accusative, object of सम्बोधयति) — 'the trees'. (d) Sage Kanva addresses the trees.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
शकुन्तला वनज्योत्स्नां लतां आलिङ्गति। सा मृगशिशुं आमन्त्रयते। तस्याः नेत्रे अश्रुपूर्णे भवतः।
(a) Which creeper does Shakuntala embrace? (b) From whom else does she take leave? (c) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'नेत्रे'. (d) What is the mood of the scene?
questions.answer: (a) She embraces the jasmine-creeper Vanajyotsna (वनज्योत्स्ना). (b) She takes leave of the fawn (मृगशिशु) she had reared. (c) नेत्रे = the two eyes. (d) The mood is one of tender sorrow — her eyes fill with tears as she parts from those she loves.
